arguments.name: Creeds predate the written Gospels
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The earliest Christian creeds were formulated and circulating before the writing of the New Testament Gospels.
premises: P1: The best-known creeds must be pre-50 AD because 1 Thessalonians, the most commonly dated early book, is usually placed around 48–50 AD.
P2: If Jesus died around 30 AD, the gap between the crucifixion and these creeds is only about 15–20 years.
P3: This places the creeds earlier than Mark and all the Gospels.

arguments.name: Paul assumes audience knowledge of creedal content
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Paul's letters presuppose that his audiences already knew the core creedal definitions about Jesus.
premises: P1: When Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, he does not define who Christ is or explain what makes him deity.
P2: He assumes his audience already knows those definitions.
P3: In a Greek culture, using 'Lord' without definition would be ambiguous unless the meaning was already established.
P4: This presupposes earlier material that predates 1 Thessalonians.

arguments.name: Other early epistles contain early creeds
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Creeds are also found in other early Pauline letters, reinforcing an early date for the oral tradition.
premises: P1: 1 Corinthians is often dated to around 53 AD and contains creedal material in 1 Corinthians 15:3 and following.
P2: Romans contains major creeds such as Romans 10:9 and Romans 1:3–4.
P3: These letters are early, so the creeds they cite must be earlier still.

arguments.name: Bart Ehrman has dated 1 Corinthians 15 creed to the 30s
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Even Bart Ehrman has classified the 1 Corinthians 15 creed as originating in the 30s AD, despite later distancing himself from that view.
premises: P1: Ehrman previously put the 1 Corinthians 15 creed in the 30s.
P2: Ehrman later said he did not mean that.
P3: Habermas has found 8–10 instances in Ehrman's writings where he says '30s,' and two or three where he says 'first two or three years.'

arguments.name: Majority of scholars date oral tradition to the 30s
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: A majority of scholars included in Habermas's volume three would place the development of the oral tradition in the 30s AD.
premises: P1: Habermas has surveyed a large number of scholars in his volumes.
P2: He states that dating the oral tradition to the 30s is very common among them.

arguments.name: Jesus Seminar admits pre-Pauline creed
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Even the Jesus Seminar, despite rejecting most of Jesus's words, acknowledges that the 1 Corinthians 15 creed existed before Paul's conversion.
premises: P1: The Jesus Seminar rejects 91% of the red-letter words of Jesus, and 82% if pink words are included.
P2: In volume two, the Jesus Seminar says that 1 Corinthians 15:3–5 or more verses is a creed Paul cites but did not author.
P3: They say the creed or its component parts existed before Paul's journey to Damascus.
P4: Paul became a Christian two to three years after the cross according to both conservatives and liberals (e.g., Bultmann).
P5: Therefore the creed existed within about two to three years of the crucifixion.

arguments.name: Paul's persecution implies early creedal knowledge
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Paul's pre-conversion persecution of the church makes sense if the early creed was already being taught.
premises: P1: Paul was 'breathing out threatenings against the church' before his conversion.
P2: He already knew what the early Christians were teaching in the creed.
P3: Romans 10:9, another early creed, contains the classic gospel of deity, death, and resurrection.
P4: If that creed was circulating before Paul's conversion, he would have been angry because it was blasphemy to him.

arguments.name: Paul's undisputed letters contain early creedal material
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The seven undisputed Pauline letters contain early creedal material, and critics grant Paul was an eyewitness.
premises: P1: Critics admit Paul was an eyewitness and generally accept the seven undisputed letters: Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon.
P2: Paul has these early verses in those letters.
P3: In Romans 10:9, Paul cites a creed and then applies an Old Testament word for Jehovah to Jesus, indicating deity.
P4: Therefore these creedal statements are very early.

arguments.name: Dating the creed to the 30s is common
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: It is very common to date the creedal tradition to the 30s AD, within the first ten years after the crucifixion.
premises: P1: The Jesus Seminar itself says the creed existed before Paul's conversion, which is at most about three years after the cross.
P2: Habermas can cite a number of scholars who date it between 30 and 39 AD.
P3: Therefore dating it anywhere in the first ten years is reasonable.
